young.html: Henri Bergson (say BERG-son) was a French thinker who asked: how many ways are there to know something?

Imagine your hometown. You could look at a hundred photographs of it, taken from every corner. Or you could walk its streets on a summer evening. Bergson said the photographs, however many, never add up to the walk. Knowing from outside, piece by piece, is one way. Knowing from inside, all at once, is another.

young.html: Outside and inside. Pick a song you love. First describe it in a list: how fast, how loud, which instruments. Then sing or hum it. Which tells you more about the song? Talk about what the list leaves out.

full.html: Henri Bergson (1859–1941) taught at the Collège de France in Paris, where his lectures drew crowds. His books on time, memory and life made him one of the most famous thinkers of his day, and he won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1927. An Introduction to Metaphysics is a long essay of 1903. The English poet and critic T. E. Hulme translated it in 1912, with Bergson checking the proofs.

full.text: A comparison of the definitions of metaphysics and the various conceptions of the absolute leads to the discovery that philosophers, in spite of their apparent divergencies, agree in distinguishing two profoundly different ways of knowing a thing. The first implies that we move round the object; the second that we enter into it.
full.author: Henri Bergson
full.ed: G. P. Putnam's Sons, New York and London

full.html: The first way Bergson calls analysis. It looks from a point of view and uses symbols: words, numbers, diagrams. It is the way of science, and it is very useful. But, he says, it always stays "relative," tied to where we stand.

full.text: By intuition is meant the kind of intellectual sympathy by which one places oneself within an object in order to coincide with what is unique in it and consequently inexpressible.
full.author: Henri Bergson
full.ed: G. P. Putnam's Sons, New York and London

full.name: gb-bergson-views
full.cap: Bergson's own example of the town, and a melody: analysis gathers more and more views or points; intuition enters the whole.

full.html: The first thing we can know from inside, Bergson says, is ourselves: our own flowing life in time, which he calls duration (durée). Clock time cuts time into equal moments, like beads on a string. Lived time is more like a melody, where each note is colored by the ones before. Analysis breaks it into pieces; intuition follows it as it flows.

full.text: Were all the photographs of a town, taken from all possible points of view, to go on indefinitely completing one another, they would never be equivalent to the solid town in which we walk about.
full.author: Henri Bergson
full.ed: G. P. Putnam's Sons, New York and London

full.html: Bergson was a celebrity before the First World War. William James admired him warmly and praised his work in print; writers and artists drew on his ideas of time and memory. Critics were sharp too. Bertrand Russell, in 1912, attacked Bergson's trust in intuition over intellect as a step away from careful reasoning. In 1922 Bergson debated Albert Einstein in Paris about whether physics had said all there is to say about time; most physicists sided with Einstein. Bergson's fame faded after the 1920s, but philosophers of process, such as Whitehead, and later French thinkers took up his questions again.
Thinking Bergson was against science. He respected it; he argued that its method of analysis, though powerful, is not the only way to know.

items: Plato and Plotinus, earlier on this ladder, also spoke of a knowing beyond step-by-step reasoning, though Bergson's "absolute" is the flow of change, not unchanging forms.
Augustine asked in the Confessions what time is, and found it in the stretching of the mind; compare Bergson's duration.
Kant argued we know things only through the forms of our own mind; Bergson thought intuition could reach further.
Whitehead, two rungs on, built a philosophy of process; Proust and Woolf, in the literature rungs, wrote novels of memory and lived time.
Is there knowledge that cannot be put into words or numbers?
Is lived time the same as clock time?
Can science explain what it is like to be you?
When is intuition a good guide, and when is it not?

questions: What is something you know "from inside" that is hard to explain to someone else?
Does an hour always feel the same length? When does time feel fast or slow?
Are photographs of a place as good as being there? What is missing?
Russell worried that trusting intuition could lead people astray. When should we check our hunches?
Can you describe a friend completely in a list of facts?
